caption:
Did phrenology ever count as real science?

Roughly 1810 to 1840, it did. Franz Joseph Gall began lecturing in 1796 and claimed the brain was an aggregate of 27 organs, each pressing its size into the skull above it. Read the bumps, read the character.

Victorian Britain loved it. George Combe's On the Constitution of Man sold more than 200,000 copies. By the 1840s London had over 28 phrenological societies. Queen Victoria and Prince Albert invited Combe to read their children's heads, and ordinary clients asked phrenologists about hiring staff and choosing a spouse.

Critics called it pseudoscience at the time. Pierre Flourens removed parts of pigeons' brains and found the losses never matched Gall's map. Paul Broca found a left frontal lesion that destroyed speech production but not comprehension. Phrenologists could not even agree how many organs there were — 27, then over 40 — or where they sat.

The afterlife was uglier. Phrenology was used to rank races, and in the 1930s Belgian colonial authorities in Rwanda used it to explain a supposed Tutsi superiority over Hutu.

What survives is Gall's one correct instinct: the brain is spatially organised, with a real division of labour. None of that organisation correlates with the shape of your skull.

Images: Lorenzo Fowler's china phrenology bust (Whipple Museum); a skull annotated by Pastor Oberlin after Gall's system; the American Phrenological Journal, 1848; an 1875 lecture poster by Samuel Robert Wells; A. S. Hartrick's 'The Phrenologist', 1895; a 1927 photograph of a skull measurement.

cards.headline: Skull shape predicts <y>nothing at all</y>
cards.note: Flourens' ablations and Broca's speech area dismantled it by 1840. Gall's one good guess: the brain really is spatially organised.
